study_identification_part.si4_title: Age-atypical brain functional networks in autism spectrum disorder: a normative modeling approach

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To use normative modeling with ABIDE resting-state fMRI data to generate individualized whole-brain network functional connectivity maps of age-related atypicality in ASD, identify deviations from typical functional network development at individual level, and explore correlations between ASD symptoms and brain networks.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: ComBat harmonization (MATLAB implementation) was used to account for site, collection time, and data acquisition parameter variability across the 17 ABIDE data collection sites. Diagnosis was treated as the biological variable of interest. Parametric prior method was used in the empirical Bayes procedure. The authors acknowledge in limitations that hierarchical Bayesian approach (HBR) may be preferable to ComBat as it avoids excluding meaningful variance correlated with site.

Extreme value distribution fitted to trimmed 1% highest absolute deviations to capture maximum deviation.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis:
Answer: Spearman correlation analyses between W-scores of each brain network and phenotypic characteristics of ASD patients (ADOS, SRS, SCQ, AQ, FIQ scores), with FDR correction for multiple comparisons (pcorrected<0.05 considered significant). Group comparisons (ASD vs TD) using outlier rates across three age groups (5-11, 12-17, 18-30 years) with ANOVA including group×age interaction. Hypothesis testing on W-scores after removing outliers (±2 SD truncation).
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: The study clearly describes the statistical methods for association analyses. Spearman correlations were used to test associations between network W-scores and behavioral measures, with FDR correction. Group comparisons examined outlier rates across age groups using ANOVA. Specific statistical values are reported in Supplement 5.
Supporting Text: We explored whether the W-scores reflected underlying phenotypic features by performing Spearman correlation analyses with the W-scores of each brain network and the phenotypic characteristics of ASD patients, such as ADOS, SRS, SCQ, AQ, and FIQ scores. After addressing multiple comparison corrections, correlation with FDR corrected p < 0.05 was considered significant. ... The significant main effect of the group indicated that the outlier rates were greater in the ASD cohort (8.07%) than in the TD cohort (3.75%) [F(11217) = 41.83, pcorrected < 0.001]. There was also a significant main effect of Age [F(2, 1217) = 75.611, pcorrected < 0.001]. Furthermore, the group × age interaction yielded a significant result [F(2, 1212) = 0.167, pcorrected = 0.015].

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief:
Answer: ASD individuals exhibit highly individualized, age-atypical functional network trajectories; outlier rates increase with age in ASD but decrease in TD; deviations correlate with severity of repetitive behaviors and social communication symptoms, particularly in DMN.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: This summary captures the three main findings emphasized in the abstract and conclusion: (1) individualized atypical trajectories, (2) divergent age-related patterns between ASD and TD, (3) clinical associations with symptoms especially in DMN.
Supporting Text: We identified a subset exhibiting highly atypical individual-level FC, exceeding 2 standard deviation from the normative value. We also identified clinically relevant networks (mainly default mode network) at cohort level, since the outlier rates decreased with age in TD participants, but increased in those with autism. Moreover, deviations were linked to severity of repetitive behaviors and social communication symptoms.
Location: materials/Jiang2024.pdf.md:L49
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed:
Answer: The study identified marked individual-level deviations in functional connectivity using normative modeling. Outlier rates (>2 SD from norm) showed distinct developmental patterns: in TD, outlier rates decreased from 6.22% (children 5-11y) to 5.21% (adolescents 12-17y) to 2.24% (adults 18-30y), whereas in ASD they increased from 4.07% to 8.32% to 15.42%. Overall outlier rates were significantly higher in ASD (8.07%) vs TD (3.75%), F(1,1217)=41.83, p<0.001, with significant group×age interaction, F(2,1212)=0.167, p=0.015. Network W-scores showed significant negative correlations with SRS subscales, strongest for DMN (SRS_awareness r=-0.192, pcorr=0.028; SRS_cognition r=-0.101, pcorr=0.025; SRS_mannerisms r=-0.153, pcorr=0.045), FPN (SRS_cognition r=-0.262, pcorr=0.001; SRS_communication r=-0.112, pcorr=0.021; SRS_mannerisms r=-0.183, pcorr=0.007), and OCN (SRS_cognition r=-0.243, pcorr=0.002; SRS_communication r=-0.145, pcorr=0.013; SRS_mannerisms r=-0.176, pcorr=0.008). Between-network FC involving DMN showed particularly strong negative correlations with multiple SRS subscales. These findings indicate that weaker functional connectivity is associated with more severe social cognitive and communication deficits in ASD.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: This detailed summary incorporates specific numerical findings reported in the Results section and Supplement 5, including outlier rate percentages, statistical test results, and correlation coefficients with p-values.
Supporting Text: See materials/Jiang2024.pdf.md:L164-L176 for outlier rate findings; L156-L158 for correlation results; materials/S0033291724000138sup005.docx.md for complete correlation table
Location: materials/Jiang2024.pdf.md:L164-L176; L156-L158; materials/S0033291724000138sup005.docx.md
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes:
Answer: Six functional networks (DMN, FPN, CON, SMN, OCN, CEN) derived from Dosenbach160 parcellation. 23 network-level W-scores computed (6 within-network + 15 between-network + 2 overall). LOESS bandwidth optimized via Brent's method (R optim function) testing 5-100% of age range. Bootstrap reliability assessment (1000 resamples). Percentile scoring and sensitivity analyses conducted. Extreme value statistics applied to capture maximum deviations (trimmed 1% highest). Age groups for some analyses: children (5-11y), adolescents (12-17y), adults (18-30y). ComBat harmonization with diagnosis as biological variable. Left-handed participants excluded. MPRAGE structural images available but not used in analyses.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: These application-specific details are described throughout the Methods section and supplements, representing notable technical and analytical choices beyond the standard extraction categories.
Supporting Text: See methods descriptions in materials/Jiang2024.pdf.md:L94-L143 and supplements

caa10_key_limitations.answer:
Answer: Cross-sectional design limits individual trajectory inference; ComBat may remove meaningful variance (HBR suggested as preferable alternative); W-scores based on two-stage mean calculations may lose precision; limited age coverage (excludes very early childhood and late adulthood); severe sex imbalance (male:female ≈5:1) limits generalizability to females; LOESS-based SD estimates potentially unstable in sparse age bins (bins with ≤2 subjects excluded); motion remains a confounding factor despite regression; choice of LOESS over other normative methods (e.g., GPR) affects model characteristics.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: These limitations are explicitly discussed in the Limitations and future directions section of the paper. The authors systematically address data limitations, methodological choices, and confounding factors.
Supporting Text: First, the current data are cross-sectional, and standardized age-modeling methods cannot make individual-level judgments about trajectories. ... researchers suggested that the hierarchical Bayesian approach may be a better alternative to ComBat ... Third, the calculation of W-scores was based on two mean calculations from the raw data, which inevitably led to some loss of precision ... Fourth, although this study has a large sample size, it does not encompass the very early developmental period or the very late adulthood period; it also has few female participants, with a male-to-female ratio of approximately 5:1 ... because it is based on an estimate of the standard deviation of the normative sample, it is potentially sensitive to small sample sizes in specific age ranges ... Finally, although head motion within scanners is a well-known confounding factor

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: Network definitions: 1=DMN (default mode network), 2=FPN (frontoparietal network), 3=CON (cingulo-opercular network), 4=SMN (sensorimotor network), 5=OCN (occipital network), 6=CEN (cerebellum network). Age groups for stratified analyses: children (5-11 years), adolescents (12-17 years), adults (18-30 years). The study excluded age bins with ≤2 TD subjects from normative model to avoid unstable SD estimates. Initial ABIDE sample: 659 ASD, 836 TD; final analyzed: 576 ASD, 642 TD. Both MPRAGE structural images and rs-fMRI available in ABIDE, but only rs-fMRI used. Supplement 3 compares LOESS vs Gaussian Process Regression, justifying LOESS choice based on computational efficiency, handling of outliers/missing data, and interpretability. Supplement 4 shows all 23 normative model maps. Supplement 5 provides complete correlation table between W-scores and SRS subscales. Code and data availability stated on GitHub (Bethlehem et al., 2018 reference). IQ data also available: ASD mean=106.1±16.41 (range 41-148), TD mean=111.47±12.23 (range 73-148). SRS scores: ASD n=482, mean=81.12±21.51 (range 6-164); TD n=457, mean=38.82±15.15 (range 0-85).
